glossary: The Article V procedure for changing the Constitution. Proposal by two-thirds of both houses of Congress or by a convention called by two-thirds of state legislatures; ratification by three-fourths of the states.
Opponents of ratification who wanted more power reserved to state governments and insisted on adding a bill of rights. Brutus No. 1 is the required example of their writing.
The first national governing document, in effect from 1781 to 1789. It created a league of states with a weak Congress, no executive, and no national judiciary.
A legislature with two chambers. The U.S. Congress is bicameral as a result of the Great Compromise.
A legislative act declaring a person guilty and imposing punishment without a trial. Prohibited to both Congress and the states.
The first ten amendments, ratified in 1791. Promised during ratification to address Anti-Federalist concerns about individual liberty.

An Anti-Federalist essay from 1787 arguing that a republic requires shared interests, that a large and diverse country cannot be represented well, and that the necessary and proper and supremacy clauses would let national power swallow the states.
The powers each branch holds to restrain the others, so that no branch becomes too powerful.
The Senate procedure for ending debate and forcing a vote. Requires 60 votes on legislation.
Article I, Section 8. Gives Congress power to regulate commerce with foreign nations, among the states, and with Indian tribes.
The 1776 document, drafted by Jefferson with help from Adams and Franklin, that restates natural rights philosophy and grounds popular sovereignty.
Government in which political power rests with the people, exercised either directly or through elected representatives.
One party controls the presidency while another controls at least one chamber of Congress.
The system in which electors chosen by each state select the president. A compromise between selection by Congress and direct popular election.
A model emphasizing limited participation, with decisions made by a small number of people holding disproportionate influence.
Powers specifically listed in the Constitution, chiefly in Article I, Section 8.
A law that criminalizes an act after the fact or increases the punishment retroactively. Prohibited to both Congress and the states.
The Article IV requirement that a state return a person charged with a crime who has fled to another state.
In Madison’s definition, a group of citizens — whether a majority or a minority — united by a common passion or interest adverse to the rights of other citizens or to the interests of the community.
The division of power between the national government and the state governments.
Madison’s essay arguing that a large republic is better than a small one at controlling the mischiefs of faction.
Madison’s essay explaining how separation of powers and checks and balances control potential abuses by majorities. Source of the line that ambition must be made to counteract ambition.
Eighty-five essays by Hamilton, Madison, and Jay, published under the name Publius, urging ratification of the Constitution.
Supporters of ratification and of a strong central government.
Prolonged debate in the Senate used to delay or block a vote. Ended only by cloture.
Article IV, Section 1. Requires each state to honor the public acts, records, and judicial proceedings of every other state.
Lincoln’s 1863 speech, delivered during the Civil War, reaffirming equality and popular sovereignty as defining foundations of democracy.
The agreement creating a bicameral Congress with the House apportioned by population and the Senate giving each state equal representation. Also called the Connecticut Compromise.

A court order requiring that a detained person be brought before a judge so the legality of the detention can be tested. The Constitution bars suspension except in cases of rebellion or invasion when public safety requires it.
The formal charging of an official with abuse of power or misconduct. The House impeaches by simple majority. Impeachment is not removal — removal requires conviction by two-thirds of the Senate.
Powers not listed in the Constitution but derived from enumerated powers through the necessary and proper clause.
The power of courts to declare acts of the other branches unconstitutional. Not stated explicitly in the Constitution; asserted by the Supreme Court in Marbury v. Madison.

The political philosophy emphasizing individual rights, limited government, consent of the governed, and private property. Note that this is the founding-era meaning, not the way the word is used in American politics today.
The ideal that a government’s power cannot be absolute.

English philosopher (1632–1704) whose Second Treatise of Civil Government argued that government rests on consent, exists to protect natural rights, and may be replaced when it fails that purpose. A major influence on the Declaration.
The Supreme Court decision establishing judicial review.
Rights that all people possess and that cannot be taken away.
The final clause of Article I, Section 8, allowing Congress to make all laws needed to carry its enumerated powers into execution. The basis of implied powers. Also called the elastic clause.
The proposal for a single legislative chamber with equal representation for every state, favored by small states.
A model emphasizing broad participation in politics and civil society.
The largest share of votes, which may still be less than half.
A model emphasizing group-based activism by nongovernmental interests competing to influence political decisions.
The ideal that all government power comes from the consent of the people.
A government in which the people elect representatives to exercise power on their behalf, with no monarch.
The principle that government derives its authority from the people and operates through elected representatives.
Powers not delegated to the national government and not prohibited to the states, which the Tenth Amendment reserves to the states or to the people.
The division of government into three branches, each with its own distinct function.
The 1786–87 uprising of indebted Massachusetts farmers who shut down county courts. The national government could not raise troops in response, exposing a key weakness of the Articles.
The agreement postponing until 1808 any decision on banning the importation of enslaved persons.
The idea that society rests on an implicit agreement in which people give up some freedoms in order to maintain social order.
Any threshold above a simple majority — three-fifths, two-thirds, or three-fourths.
Article VI. Makes the Constitution, federal laws, and treaties the supreme law of the land, binding state judges.
Article II, Section 3. Requires the president to take care that the laws be faithfully executed.
Reserves to the states, or to the people, those powers not delegated to the national government nor prohibited to the states.
The formula counting three-fifths of a state’s enslaved population for purposes of representation in the House and for direct taxation.
A majority using its numbers to override the rights of a minority — the danger Madison addresses in Federalist No. 10.
The proposal for a bicameral legislature with representation in both chambers based on population, favored by large states.
